Fig. 7 presents P50/P90/P95/P99 latency on SIFT1M. FAISS sustains sub-2 ms latency at all percentiles, and its bars are visibly the flattest in the chart, the clearest indicator of tail-latency consistency among the seven systems. Among databases, Qdrant is both fastest (4.55 ms P50) and most consistent (P99/P50 = 1.85); pgvector shows the tightest tail ratio (1.63) despite higher absolute latency, meaning its worstcase queries are proportionally closer to its typical query than any other database, a desirable property for SLA-bound deployments even though its median is not the lowest. Milvus (2.04) and Weaviate (1.94) show the largest tail-to-median spread, consistent with their distributed, multi-stage query paths introducing occasional latency spikes not present in simpler single-process architectures.

Fig. 5. Query throughput (QPS, log scale) on SIFT1M. FAISS leads by 416× over full database systems; Qdrant leads among databases.

Fig. 6. Query throughput across all six datasets (log scale). Throughput drops 2-5× on the 960-dimensional GIST1M relative to lower-dimensional sets.

## D. Index Build Time and Resource Usage

Fig. 7. Latency percentiles (P50/P90/P95/P99) by database on SIFT1M. FAISS is fastest and most consistent; Qdrant leads among full databases.

## E. Trade-off Analysis

Fig. 10 visualizes the recall-throughput trade-off on SIFT1M. Systems form four regimes: a high-throughput regime (FAISS: 866 QPS, 0.907 recall); a balanced regime (Qdrant: 216 QPS/0.959 recall; pgvector: 154/0.937; Chroma: 133/0.912); a quality-focused regime (Weaviate: 87/0.996; Milvus: 88/0.954); and an efficiency-focused regime

Fig. 9. Peak RAM (left) and index size (right) on SIFT1M. LanceDB and FAISS lead in RAM; pgvector is the storage outlier.

Fig. 11. Impact of embedding dimensionality on (a) throughput and (b) recall. All systems degrade on the 960-dimensional GIST1M; Milvus degrades least.

Fig. 10. Recall@100 vs. QPS on SIFT1M (log scale). Systems separate into high-throughput, balanced, quality-focused, and efficiency-focused regimes.

## C. Query Throughput and Latency

Fig. 5 shows single-threaded throughput on SIFT1M. FAISS reaches 866 QPS, 4-16× higher than the full database systems, because it bypasses network, serialization, and transactional overhead as an in-process library. Among databases, Qdrant leads (216 QPS), followed by pgvector (154), Chroma (133), Milvus and Weaviate (∼87-88), and LanceDB (53), whose disk-based architecture is the slowest; notably, the two systems with the highest recall in Fig. 1 (Weaviate and Milvus) occupy the bottom half of the throughput ranking, an early signal of the recall-throughput tension explored quantitatively in Section IVD.

Fig. 3. NDCG@100 across all database-dataset pairs. Darker green indicates higher ranking quality. FAISS leads overall; pgvector is weakest on Random and GIST1M.

Fig. 4. (a) Precision@10 and (b) MRR by dataset. Most systems score near 1.0 on both; LanceDB trails on GIST1M.

Figure 8: Left: Throughput (QPS) for out-of-distribution and in-distribution queries on the laion-clip dataset at 95% average recall; middle: PCA projections comparing the corpus with in-distribution queries (top) and out-of-distribution queries (bottom).

## 5.4 Significance tests

To assess the robustness of our results, for each dataset we select each algorithm's fastest configuration reaching at least 95% average recall and compare algorithms using their paired per-query latencies over the 1000 test queries. We test all pairwise differences using Wilcoxon signed rank tests (Wilcoxon, 1945) with the Holm-Bonferroni correction (Holm, 1979). Almost all (2399 out of 2450 pairwise comparisons 8 of algorithms reaching 95% average recall) of the differences are statistically significant at the significance level α = 0.01. The critical difference diagrams (Demšar, 2006) visualizing the results of the significance tests for agnews-mxbai and arxiv-nomic can be found in Figure 11.

Figure 11: Critical difference diagrams visualizing the results of the significance tests for the agnews-mxbai and arxiv-nomic datasets. The bold horizontal black bars connect the algorithms whose paired per-query latency differences are not statistically significant at the level α = 0.01 (with Holm-Bonferroni correction).

We report recall here to maintain consistency with the other ANN workloads.
details.response:
Based on empirical benchmark studies and comparative performance evaluations, here is the detailed comparison of **index build times** and **latency percentiles (P50, P95, P99)** between **Qdrant** and **Weaviate**.

---

### 1. Comparative Performance Overview

| Metric / Dimension | Qdrant | Weaviate | Analysis & Architectural Factors |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Index Build Time (SIFT1M)** | **194.7 seconds** | **474.9 seconds** | Qdrant builds its HNSW graph ~2.4× faster. Weaviate spends significantly more time building due to higher-quality default HNSW parameters. |
| **P50 Latency (SIFT1M)** | **4.55 ms** | *Higher than Qdrant* | Qdrant is the fastest full database engine at median latency (P50). |
| **Tail Latency Ratio (P99 / P50 on SIFT1M)** | **1.85** | **1.94** | Qdrant demonstrates tighter tail-latency consistency. Weaviate exhibits a wider spread due to multi-stage query processing overhead. |
| **Throughput / QPS (SIFT1M)** | **216 QPS** | **87 QPS** | Qdrant delivers ~2.5× higher query throughput in single-threaded evaluations. |
| **Recall / Precision Trade-off (SIFT1M)** | **0.959 Recall** | **0.996 Recall** | Weaviate operates in a quality-focused regime (trading build time and throughput for near-perfect recall), while Qdrant operates in a balanced regime. |
| **Upload + Index Time (dbpedia-openai-1M)** | **24.43 min** *(Upload: 3.51 m)* | **13.94 min** *(Upload: 13.94 m)* | In this multi-threaded high-dimensional run (1536-d, scalar quantization setup), Weaviate indexed inline during upload, whereas Qdrant deferred full post-indexing optimization. |
| **Latency: Mean (dbpedia-openai-1M)** | **3.54 ms** | **4.99 ms** | Qdrant achieves ~29% lower average latency. |
| **Latency: P95 (dbpedia-openai-1M)** | **4.95 ms** | **7.16 ms** | Qdrant maintains lower 95th percentile latency. |
| **Latency: P99 (dbpedia-openai-1M)** | **8.62 ms** | **11.33 ms** | Qdrant achieves ~24% lower tail latency (P99). |

---

### 2. Key Insights and Architectural Trade-offs

* **Index Construction Speed:**
  * In standard HNSW evaluations on SIFT1M (128-dimensional vectors), **Qdrant** constructed its index in **194.7 s**, benefiting from its native Rust implementation and single-node memory layout. 
  * **Weaviate** took **474.9 s** (~2.44× longer), as its indexing routine builds denser graph connectivity by default to maximize recall.
* **Latency Profile and Tail Consistency:**
  * **Median Latency (P50):** On SIFT1M, Qdrant led all tested vector database systems with a median latency of **4.55 ms**.
  * **Tail Latency (P99):** Qdrant demonstrated high predictability with a tail-to-median ratio ($P_{99}/P_{50}$) of **1.85**. In contrast, Weaviate registered a higher spread ratio of **1.94**, attributed to its multi-stage query path introducing occasional tail latency spikes under concurrent loads.
  * In high-dimensional workloads (`dbpedia-openai-1M-1536-angular`), Qdrant sustained lower latency across all tiers (**3.54 ms mean**, **4.95 ms P95**, **8.62 ms P99**) compared to Weaviate (**4.99 ms mean**, **7.16 ms P95**, **11.33 ms P99**).
* **Throughput vs. Recall Regimes:**
  * Benchmark clustering places **Qdrant** in the *balanced regime* (higher QPS of 216 with 0.959 recall on SIFT1M), while **Weaviate** sits in the *quality-focused regime* (lower QPS of 87 with 0.996 recall), reflecting distinct default parameter priorities between build/query speed and recall maximization.

---

### Sources
* *Academic Vector Database Benchmark Study: Section IV-C ("Query Throughput and Latency", Fig. 5 & Fig. 7) & Section IV-D ("Index Build Time and Resource Usage", Fig. 8 & Fig. 10).*
* *Qdrant Vector Database Benchmarks (Dataset: `dbpedia-openai-1M-1536-angular`, 100 search threads).*
details.reference: On SIFT1M, Qdrant outperforms Weaviate in index build time (194.7 s vs. 474.9 s) and median latency (4.55 ms P50, with a P99/P50 ratio of 1.85 compared to Weaviate's 1.94 due to multi-stage query overhead). On dbpedia-openai-1M-1536-angular, Qdrant achieves 3.54 ms mean latency and 8.62 ms P99 latency (Upload Time: 3.51 min, Upload + Index Time: 24.43 min), whereas Weaviate records 4.99 ms mean latency and 11.33 ms P99 latency (Upload + Index Time: 13.94 min).

## 5 Performance evaluation

## 5.1 Experimental setup

Each experiment is run on a compute node with 384 GB of RAM and two Intel Xeon Gold 6230 (Cascade Lake) CPUs. Each CPU has 20 cores and supports AVX-512 instructions. All algorithms are benchmarked using a single worker thread on one physical CPU core, with simultaneous multithreading (SMT) disabled, and we use numactl to bind the algorithm execution to one CPU socket and constrain memory allocation to its associated local NUMA node. All of the compared implementations are written in C++ with the exception of PyNNDescent (Dong et al., 2011; McInnes, 2018), which uses the Numba library extensively for just-in-time compilation. All implementations are heavily optimized and use techniques such as vectorization to accelerate distance computations.

By default, we use k = 100 in all experiments because it is representative of real-world applications: retrieval systems commonly retrieve more candidates than they ultimately return, allowing the candidates to be filtered, diversified, or reranked using more expensive models. We use average recall to measure the effectiveness and queries per second (QPS) to measure the efficiency of the algorithms. Each query hyperparameter combination is run five times, and we use the minimum query time across these runs to compute QPS.
